Judicial Law and General Equity
joo-DISH-ul LAW and JEN-er-ul EK-wi-tee
noun phrase (Reformed theology)
The Reformed-confessional doctrine (Westminster Confession XIX.4) that the judicial (civil) law given to national Israel expired with the Israelite state, except for its general equity — the underlying just principles that continue to inform the civil order. Distinguished from theonomy (which would apply the Mosaic judicial law more directly).

📖 Biblical Definition

The Reformed-confessional doctrine (Westminster Confession XIX.4) governing the contemporary status of the judicial (civil) law of Moses. The judicial law comprises the civil-legal code given to Israel as a national-theocratic body: the laws of property, contracts, courts, punishments, civil administration, and national life. Westminster XIX.4 states: To them also, as a body politic, he gave sundry judicial laws, which expired together with the State of that people; not obliging any other now, further than the general equity thereof may require. The substantive doctrine has two parts. (1) The specific Israelite-theocratic judicial laws expired with national Israel: the particular civil applications given to Israel as a national-theocratic body (the specific penalties, the specific civil arrangements, the specific theocratic provisions) are not binding on other nations now, because they were given to Israel as a unique national-theocratic body that has passed away with the coming of Christ and the dissolution of the OT theocracy. (2) The general equity continues to oblige: the underlying just principles embedded in the judicial law (the general equity, the substantive justice the laws expressed) continue to inform the civil order and to instruct the Christian magistrate. For example, the specific Mosaic law requiring a parapet around a flat roof (Deuteronomy 22:8) is not binding as a specific civil statute, but its general equity (the principle that one must take reasonable measures to prevent harm to others on one's property) continues to oblige. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive general-equity doctrine, distinguishing it from two opposing positions. Theonomy (the Reconstructionist position of R. J. Rushdoony, Greg Bahnsen, and others) would apply the Mosaic judicial law (including its specific penalties) more directly and comprehensively to the modern civil order. The natural-law-only position would derive civil justice from natural law without substantive reference to the Mosaic judicial law. The general-equity position holds the substantive middle: the specific Mosaic judicial laws are not binding statutes, but their general equity continues to instruct the civil order, and the Mosaic judicial law remains a substantive source of wisdom for the Christian magistrate alongside natural law.

JUDICIAL LAW AND GENERAL EQUITY, n. phr. (Reformed theology) Westminster Confession XIX.4: the judicial (civil) law given to national Israel expired together with the State of that people; not obliging any other now, further than the general equity thereof may require. Two parts: (1) the specific Israelite-theocratic judicial laws expired with national Israel (the particular penalties, civil arrangements, theocratic provisions not binding on other nations now); (2) the general equity continues to oblige (the underlying just principles, the substantive justice the laws expressed, continue to inform the civil order). Distinguished from theonomy (Rushdoony, Bahnsen; more direct application of the judicial law) and the natural-law-only position. The judicial law remains a source of wisdom for the Christian magistrate alongside natural law.

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The general-equity doctrine is held between theonomy (which applies the Mosaic judicial law more directly) and the natural-law-only position; the Reformed-confessional position holds that the specific judicial laws expired but their general equity continues to instruct the civil order.

expand to see more

The general-equity doctrine holds the substantive Reformed-confessional middle between two positions. Theonomy (the Christian Reconstructionist position of R. J. Rushdoony, Greg Bahnsen, and others) holds that the Mosaic judicial law, including its specific penalties, remains binding on the civil magistrate in exhaustive detail, except where explicitly abrogated by the NT; this position would apply the specific Mosaic civil penalties (including the capital sanctions for various crimes) more directly to the modern state. The natural-law-only position would derive civil justice from natural law and general revelation without substantive reference to the Mosaic judicial law. The Westminster general-equity position holds the substantive middle: the specific Israelite-theocratic judicial laws expired with national Israel (they were given to Israel as a unique national-theocratic body that has passed away), but their general equity — the underlying just principles, the substantive justice they expressed — continues to oblige and to instruct the civil order. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive general-equity doctrine: the Mosaic judicial law is not a binding civil statute-book for modern nations, but it is a substantive source of wisdom and justice for the Christian magistrate, its general equity continuing to instruct the civil order alongside natural law and general revelation. The substantive task is to discern the abiding general equity (the just principle) embedded in each Mosaic judicial law and to apply that equity wisely to the contemporary civil order, neither woodenly imposing the specific Israelite-theocratic statute nor ignoring the Mosaic judicial law as a source of civil wisdom.
